title: Average-Case Complexity of the Euclidean Algorithm

insights: Lamé's theorem is tight: consecutive Fibonacci numbers achieve the exact worst-case step count
euclideanSteps is translation-invariant: steps(a + kb, b) = steps(a, b) for any k
When a < b, the algorithm takes one extra step: steps(a,b) = steps(b,a) + 1
When b divides a, the algorithm takes exactly 1 step
Steps = 1 implies a % b = 0 (one-step termination characterization)
The 5-digit bound requires b < 10^20 because fib_ge_pow10 is verified by interval_cases up to k=20
Dixon's average-case theorem requires continued fractions, Gauss map, and ergodic theory - all absent from Mathlib v4.26.0
The full distribution (Hensley 1994, variance computation) is even further from formalizability
Steps ≤ b gives a crude but useful O(b) bound, proved by well-founded induction on euclideanSteps.induct
GCD step invariant: gcd(b, a%b) = gcd(a,b) proved via Nat.gcd_comm + Nat.gcd_rec chain
Lamé tight characterization: fib(n+1) is simultaneously a lower bound AND achieved as equality
For coprime inputs with b > 1, steps ≥ 2 since b cannot divide a
Fixed build error: euclideanSteps_swap proof had redundant rw after the goal was already closed
